rules.statement: When persisting a JSON snapshot that is compared or fingerprinted later, write its properties in a deterministic order (for example ordinal order of the names) using the application's configured JSON serializer options.
rules.why: The recorded settings are written as one JSON object in ordinal name order with the environment's JSON options, so the record can be read back and compared reliably.
rules.check: Look for snapshot or fingerprint serialization that iterates a dictionary or hash set in unspecified order, or that uses default JsonSerializerOptions instead of the configured ones.

rules.statement: When a persisted record that only serves as an optimization cannot be deserialized, catch the JsonException, log it with a dedicated log event, and fall back to the full, unoptimized behavior instead of failing.
rules.why: An unreadable reconciled-settings record is logged as ReconciledServerSettingsUnreadable and treated as absent, so the pass reconciles every tenant and still converges.
rules.check: Look for deserialization of persisted optimization state that lets a JsonException propagate and abort the operation, or that swallows it without logging.

rules.statement: A store method that records the outcome of a background pass must update only the fields it owns, and only while the row is unchanged since the pass read it (an optimistic-concurrency condition).
rules.why: UpdateReconciledSettingsAsync records the fingerprint and settings and nothing else, only while the server row is unchanged, so a concurrent settings write is not overwritten or marked reconciled by mistake.
rules.check: Look for store updates from a reconciliation or background job that overwrite the whole entity, or that write without a concurrency token or row-version check.

rules.statement: When deciding whether a server-level settings change affects a tenant or client, compare that scope's resolved effective settings before and after the change, not the raw server-level values.
rules.why: Tenant overrides, security profiles and merges decide which server settings reach a tenant, so only the effective value reliably shows whether a change reaches it.
rules.check: Look for change-impact logic that diffs server-level settings and infers which tenants are affected without resolving each tenant's effective settings under both the old and new values.
